November 17, 2026

Does the Stock Market Stigmatize Banks that Borrow from the Fed?

Natalia Fischl-Lanzoni, Martin Hiti, and Asani Sarkar

Banks may resist borrowing from the Federal Reserve during a panic if such borrowing is stigmatized (that is, viewed by the market as a sign of financial weakness), thus hampering the Fed’s ability to resolve the crisis. The problem may be particularly acute for publicly traded banks since their stock prices immediately reflect the market’s opinion of them. In this post, based on a recent paper, we track what happened to stock investors’ perceptions of a bank’s risk level right after it first borrowed from Fed facilities in the first month of the bank run of 2023. We find that, after a first trip to the Fed’s Discount Window (DW), investors became more sensitive to that bank’s weaknesses. In contrast, investors did not evince such concern when the bank took a first loan from a new facility, the Bank Term Funding Program (BTFP).

Can Workers Predict Job Finding and Job Loss?

Richard Audoly, Ivy Chen, Miles Guerin, and Rachel Schuh

Workers’ perceptions of the labor market may differ from aggregate labor market statistics. Individuals might be overly optimistic about their chance of finding a job, or too pessimistic about the odds of losing their current position. In this post, we compare subjective beliefs of future job-finding and job-loss from the New York Fed’s Survey of Consumer Expectations (SCE) with their realized counterparts in the Current Population Survey (CPS). We then investigate how closely aggregate perceptions of job-finding and job-loss prospects align with realized rates.

Banking System Vulnerability: 2026 Update

Matteo Crosignani, Thomas M. Eisenbach, and Fulvia Fringuellotti

As in previous years, we provide in this post an update on the vulnerability of the U.S. banking system based on four analytical models that capture different aspects of this vulnerability. We use data through 2026:Q2 to update our analysis and discuss how the vulnerability measures have changed since our last update one year ago.

A Look at the Wider Divide in Credit Card Delinquency by Income

Donghoon Lee, Daniel Mangrum, Joelle W. Scally, Tejas Sinha, and Wilbert van der Klaauw

Credit card delinquency rose sharply between 2022 and 2024, and the increase was steepest among borrowers in lower-income neighborhoods. Here, we check in on credit card performance by neighborhood income and trace when the borrowers who are now struggling with their payments were issued cards. We find that during the pandemic, an increasing share of new credit cards went to borrowers with lower incomes and credit scores, and those accounts are now showing higher levels of distress.

Has U.S. Monetary Policy Really Improved? A 150‑Year Perspective

Regis Barnichon and Geert Mesters

Has U.S. monetary policy actually improved over time? Or was the apparent success of the modern Federal Reserve mostly the result of more favorable economic conditions and better luck? In this post, we summarize our paper,* which develops a framework for comparing monetary policy across different economic environments. Our approach asks how close policy came to the best response given the economic conditions and shocks policymakers faced. Applying this framework to 150 years of U.S. monetary history, we find that meaningful improvements in monetary policy occurred only in the last thirty years. Most of the gains reflect, among other developments, substantially better responses to financial shocks and supply shocks.

November 5, 2026

The U.S. Oil Sector’s Role in Restraining Prices

Thomas Klitgaard

The start of the Middle East conflict in early 2026 caused an unprecedented drop in global petroleum supply. In response, oil prices jumped—but not to unprecedentedly high levels. The U.S. oil sector was a key factor in moderating the shock. For one, its steady increases in drilling helped create a large oversupply in the global market before the conflict, making it less of a challenge to offset the drop in Middle East oil output. In addition, U.S. commercial and government inventories were rapidly drawn down, filling half the gap between global supply and demand in the second quarter by some estimates. Inventories, though, are a limited resource and U.S. stockpiles stopped falling in July. As a consequence, the continued shortfall in global production has been managed by running down inventories in the rest of the world.

How Market Position Shapes Credit Card Interest Rates

Kyle Herkenhoff and Juan M. Morelli

Why is it that two borrowers who look much alike can be offered very different rates when applying for a credit card? In a recent paper, we address this question by examining how the rate offered changes when the lender’s funding cost falls. Data on 14 million newly issued cards show that when a lender’s funding costs decline, the lender passes less of that decline on to the offer rate when it holds a large market share. That is, two borrowers with similar credit scores and incomes borrowing from the same lender can see noticeably different interest rates on the credit card they are applying for.

How Do Banking Supervisors Deal with Failing Banks?

Sergio Correia, Stephan Luck, and Emil Verner

In this post, we discuss insights from a recent staff report on the role of banking supervision in identifying and disciplining failing banks. We show that bank failures typically result from supervisory closure decisions based on hard information about book equity. Yet hard information is itself partly produced by supervision, as our evidence suggests that supervisors require troubled banks to recognize potential losses. We argue that supervision faces a trade-off: Stricter supervision can reduce the costs of resolving failing banks, but it can also lead to tighter regulatory capital constraints and hold back credit supply.
